analysis.one_liner: Repeals corporate income, estate, and gift taxes and taxes only wages at 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 26, 1993, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the corporate income tax, the alternative minimum tax on corporations, the estate and gift taxes, and most special taxes on financial firms, and replaced individual income tax with a flat 10% levy on earned income above a $10,000 exemption [S2][S3]. Because the tax would apply only to wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings, income from investments, capital gains, interest, and pensions would go untaxed [S3]. All individual deductions and credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit, would be repealed [S3]. The bill got no action in committee and no vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, large financial firms, and the owners of large estates and investment wealth. Corporations would stop paying income tax entirely, and income from capital gains, dividends, and interest would not be taxed at all under the bill's earned-income-only definition [S3]. Estates would no longer face the estate or gift tax, a benefit concentrated in the largest inheritances [S3]. High earners would also gain from the flat 10% rate replacing progressive rates.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate income tax and corporate alternative minimum tax outright, along with taxes on life insurers, other insurers, mutual funds, REITs, savings banks, and foreign corporations' U.S. business income [S3].
Taxes only earned income (wages, salaries, self-employment earnings) at 10% above a $10,000 exemption, leaving capital gains, dividends, interest, and pensions untaxed [S3].
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes for decedents dying and transfers made after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working people. The bill raises no tax on investment income or corporations while repealing all deductions and credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit that low-wage workers rely on, and the federal revenue loss would force higher deficits or cuts to public services. Wage earners would carry the entire income tax burden.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners and users of public services

drawbacks.text: The bill is not revenue-neutral by any visible mechanism: it repeals the corporate tax, estate and gift taxes, and taxes on several financial sectors while imposing only a 10% tax on wages above $10,000, which would produce a large drop in federal revenue [S2][S3].
Repealing all individual deductions and credits would eliminate the Earned Income Tax Credit, which supplements the wages of low-income working families [S3].

The earned-income definition excludes pensions and annuities entirely, so a retiree with substantial retirement income would pay no income tax while a worker earning the same amount would; it also leaves voluntary tips untaxed while taxing mandatory ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's simplification appeal — one low rate, no deductions — is real on paper, but the design fails an honest cost test: it taxes only wages while eliminating taxes on corporations, estates, and nearly all capital income, and it repeals the credits that support low-wage workers. The burden would shift heavily toward people who earn their income from a paycheck.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by Sen. Helms with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Jesse Helms introduced the Flat Tax Act of 1993 in the Senate on January 26, 1993 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote during the 103rd Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tax code stayed as it was: working families kept their existing deductions and credits, and the Treasury kept the revenue from corporate, estate, and capital income taxes that the bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes on the bill, no partisan pattern can be measured; the bill attracted no support from either party.

industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax and the corporate alternative minimum tax entirely, so corporate profits would go untaxed at the federal level. The revenue would either disappear from the budget or be replaced by taxes on wage earners.

Estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would be repealed, benefiting the largest inheritances, and because only earned income is taxed, capital gains, dividends, and interest would go untaxed entirely.

industries.industry: Insurance companies, mutual funds, REITs, and savings banks
industries.note: The bill names these sectors specifically, repealing the taxes on life insurers, other insurers, regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and mutual savings banks. Their earnings would face no federal income tax.
